Privileged-Dreamer.narr: Real robots have properties (mass, friction, motor compliance) that simulators guess wrong. This paper extends Dreamer with privileged state: the world model explicitly imagines hidden physics parameters (inferred from real data) and uses those to adapt its dynamics predictions, bridging simulation and reality without changing the policy.
Privileged-Dreamer.how:
The mechanism: (1) Fit a physics simulator to real robot data and extract inferred parameters (mass, friction, spring constant). (2) Extend the world model to include these as latent state variables, predicted alongside position/velocity. (3) During imagination, the model predicts both the standard state and the hidden parameters as they evolve. (4) A policy trained on these 'privileged' rollouts learns to be reliable to parameter variation. (5) On the real robot, the learned policy works because its training used realistic parameters.

Why it works: Explicitly imagining hidden physics lets the model capture the real robot's behavior without explicit sim-to-real transfer. The policy learns on rollouts that already account for what makes reality different from the simulator.

PIP-Loco.narr: Legged robots walking on rough terrain face infinite-horizon problems: one misstep cascades into a fall. Standard model-predictive control re-plans every tick over a short horizon, but a quadruped needs to see farther ahead—past the next footstep—to commit safely. This paper integrates a learned world model into infinite-horizon MPC, letting the planner look as far as the model stays accurate.
PIP-Loco.how:
The mechanism: Encode proprioception and terrain height maps into a latent state; train a Dreamer-style RNN to predict the next state given action and hidden stochastic variables. At control time, sample thousands of candidate action sequences (gaits, step timings, foot placements) and roll each through the dynamics. Score each by the predicted reward (reach goal, no fall). Solve the infinite-horizon cost via dynamic-programming value-iteration in imagination.

Why it works: The learned model captures terrain-dependent stability that hand-tuned physics engines miss. By planning over true dynamics instead of a simplified model, the planner commits to longer horizons and recovers from partial missteps—cutting replanning overhead and enabling smooth, energy-efficient gaits on unmapped terrain.

SR-AIF.narr: Sparse-reward continuous control is hard: the robot gets reward only on success, and random exploration takes forever to stumble onto it. Most learning algorithms collapse. This paper marries active inference—choosing actions to minimize uncertainty—with a learned world model. The robot doesn't just learn what to do; it actively explores what it's unsure about, using the dream to probe hypothetical futures and navigate toward high-information regions.
SR-AIF.how:
The mechanism: Maintain a learned generative world model (encoder, dynamics, decoder) and a distribution over latent state. At each step, compute the mutual information between candidate actions and reducing state uncertainty (active inference). Prefer actions that would most tighten the belief. Roll those actions through the model; sample the stochastic component; use the predicted observation to tighten belief. With high certainty, greedily maximize predicted reward.

Why it works: Active inference turns uncertainty into signal instead of noise. Sparse-reward environments are informationally starved—the robot must learn that touching the goal is reward. By prioritizing high-information actions (e.g., "is the goal here or there?"), the agent builds accurate models much faster than random exploration, and sparse rewards guide the learned model to reward-bearing regions.

LUMOS.narr: Vision-language models can understand "pick up the red cube" from pixels, but they are trained on diverse internet data—not your robot's embodiment or gripper. This paper decouples perception from action: the language model reasons abstractly ("the goal is to move red near blue"), while a latent world model handles the robot's actual dynamics and morphology. Language priors guide the learning, but physics is learned from data.
LUMOS.how:
The mechanism: Encode observations into a latent state space with learned dynamics. Use a frozen vision-language model to extract goal predicates from the language instruction. In a latent-space MPC loop, optimize for configurations predicted to satisfy those predicates, subject to the learned dynamics. Pretrain on offline demonstrations, then fine-tune on real interaction—minimally, because language priors compress the learning problem.

Why it works: Language provides high-level task structure (goals, relationships) without entangling it to any embodiment. The learned world model captures the specific robot's dynamics and morphology offline, then policy search (in imagination) aligns language goals to real actions. This separation allows zero-shot transfer: the same language objective and world model work on different robots.

Mastering the Labyrinth.narr: Standard world models reconstruct everything: every detail in the scene, every light bounce, every texture. But for control, most of that is noise. This paper asks: reconstruct only what moves. Mask away static walls, only model the agent's position and velocity (the part that matters for planning). The result: a model that needs only 1.5 hours of real robot data instead of 5.
Mastering the Labyrinth.how:
The mechanism: Learn a scene decomposition: static background and dynamic foreground (the agent). Train the encoder to produce a latent state that recovers only the dynamic part on decoding; skip the walls. Dynamics predict the next position and velocity from action. During imagination, roll the agent forward without reconstructing irrelevant detail. Use the learned latent model for planning, and only periodically touch the real robot to refine the decomposition.

Why it works: By ignoring static scene details, the model has fewer degrees of freedom to fit, so its gradient signals are stronger and its sample efficiency rockets. The reconstruction bottleneck is broken: instead of modeling photorealism, the model focuses on the one thing that changes, making real-world learning practical for long-horizon tasks.

Planning with Adaptive World Models.narr: Every agent moves differently: a car has momentum, a drone is nimble, a robot arm is ponderous. A world model trained on one agent's behavior won't predict another's. This paper learns agent-specific motion models on the fly, allowing a single world-model architecture to adapt its predictions to whichever embodiment is doing the acting right now.
Planning with Adaptive World Models.how:
The mechanism: Encode ego motion (the agent's trajectory) and the scene layout separately. Train a dynamics model conditioned on both the latent state and an agent descriptor (e.g., a learned embedding or observed velocity profile). During planning, roll out action sequences using the appropriate agent descriptor. For a new agent, collect a few seconds of data (or infer descriptors from initial actions) and adapt the model on the fly.

Why it works: Agent descriptors capture the embodiment's mass, actuators, and control authority without explicit specification. By factoring dynamics = scene + agent-specific kinematics, the model generalizes across embodiments. Planning with MPC then respects each agent's true dynamics instead of forcing a one-size-fits-all model.

Bounding Distributional Shifts through N.narr: A learned world model is dangerous when asked to predict far outside its training data. The robot could confidently hallucinate an action that works in the dream but fails catastrophically in reality. This paper bolts a VAE-based unfamiliarity detector onto the MPC loop, flagging out-of-distribution state-action pairs and vetoing risky imagined actions before they're executed.
Bounding Distributional Shifts through N.how:
The mechanism: Train a VAE on state-action pairs from the training dataset. During planning, for each candidate action sequence, roll it through the dynamics and compute the VAE reconstruction loss at each imagined step. High loss = anomalous. If the sequence ventures into high-anomaly regions, downweight or discard it. Keep only sequences that the model was trained to understand.

Why it works: Unfamiliarity detection grounds planning in reality by refusing to commit to predictions the model was never trained on. The VAE reconstruction loss is a principled OOD signal. MPC becomes conservative exactly where it should: when the dream encounters configurations unlike the training set, it retreats to safer, more-practiced behaviors.

Online Residual Model Learning.narr: Physics changes during deployment: a robot's joints wear, the floor gets wet, wind picks up. A world model frozen at training time becomes stale. This paper keeps the base model static but learns a learnable residual on top—a small network that corrects for drift. The robot adapts online, in the control loop, without retraining.
Online Residual Model Learning.how:
The mechanism: Train a base world model offline (e.g., neural network or physics simulator). At runtime, maintain a learned residual model (another small network) that predicts the error: (true next state) − (predicted next state). Update the residual online using recent experience. When rolling out for MPC, add both predictions: ŷ = base(s,a) + residual(s,a). Adapt the residual every few steps.

Why it works: The residual captures slow, smooth changes (wear, environmental shift) without destabilizing the base model. Continuous adaptation keeps MPC aligned with current dynamics. Because the residual is small, online learning is cheap and stable—no catastrophic forgetting, no need for a fresh dataset.

Learning Active Tactile Perception throu.narr: Touch gives the robot information that vision can't: compliance, friction, whether the object is hollow. But the robot must decide where to poke before it knows what it will learn. This paper fuses a generative world model with belief-space MPC: the robot plans touches that most reduce uncertainty about the object's properties, using imagination to score which poke is most informative.
Learning Active Tactile Perception throu.how:
The mechanism: Learn a generative dynamics model (encoder-decoder RNN) that predicts the next tactile observation (force, skin deformation) given action and belief state. Maintain a Bayesian belief over object properties (compliance, mass, friction). At each step, enumerate candidate touch locations and roll forward the consequences for each, computing the posterior uncertainty about properties under each trajectory. Choose the action that most tightens the posterior.

Why it works: Touch is information-seeking: the robot's goal is not immediate success but learning quickly. By planning in belief space—where trajectories reduce uncertainty—the robot converges on object properties much faster than reactive touching. The learned model predicts what new touch data will teach, enabling the robot to self-supervise its own exploration.

Attention Surgery.narr: Video diffusion models generate stunning frames but run in real-time only on GPUs with massive memory. The bottleneck is attention's quadratic cost: O(n²) in sequence length. This paper performs linearised attention on the diffusion transformer's cross-attention—keeping the model's quality but slashing computation by ~6×.
Attention Surgery.how:
The mechanism: Replace standard dot-product attention (softmax(QK^T)V) with linear-attention approximations: replace the softmax with a learned gating function, or use kernel methods to compute attention in linear time. In a video-generation model, apply this primarily to the cross-attention between keyframes and denoised content, keeping self-attention exact where coherence matters most.

Why it works: Linear attention trades some expressiveness for speed, but for video diffusion (where the model is overly expressive anyway), the loss is imperceptible. The 6× speedup comes from reducing quadratic distance computations to linear passes. Fast generation means longer imagined rollouts in planning loops and more practical sim-like interactions.

VMonarch.narr: Transformers attend to every token with every other token, O(n²) cost. For video, n can be thousands. This paper replaces the dense attention matrix with structured Monarch-matrix patterns—a learned, data-dependent factorization that keeps 90% of expressiveness while cutting the cost to sub-quadratic.
VMonarch.how:
The mechanism: Decompose the attention weight matrix as a product of learned permutation and block-diagonal matrices (Monarch matrices). Instead of computing full attention, compute: A = P₁ ⊙ (D₁ ⊗ D₂) ⊙ P₂, where Ps are permutations and Ds are diagonal. This factorization is learned end-to-end. For video generation, apply it to both spatial and temporal attention.

Why it works: Monarch factorizations are surprisingly expressive—they capture the key dependencies (nearby tokens, temporal continuity) while skipping the long-tail quadratic cost. Applied to video diffusion, this sub-quadratic pattern keeps the generated frames coherent and detailed but runs on smaller hardware, enabling longer imagined episodes.

D2Cache.narr: Video generation is iterative: the model denoises step-by-step from noise to a frame. Every denoising step recomputes attention from scratch. But the attention map changes smoothly—a tiny increment at each step. This paper caches the denoising trajectory and interpolates, amortizing computation across steps by ~10×.
D2Cache.how:
The mechanism: After the first full denoising pass, store the attention maps and feature activations. On subsequent refinement steps, interpolate (or extrapolate) the cached trajectory forward slightly, recomputing only the incremental changes. For video, cache across time: frame t's attention is similar to frame t−1's, so predict the delta and add it.

Why it works: The denoising trajectory is smooth, so cached + delta is nearly exact. By skipping redundant computation in tight loops, the decoder runs 10× faster. Faster decoding multiplies the number of imagined steps the robot can roll during planning, or trades latency for longer videos per tick.

VideoWorld 2.narr: Video diffusion models entangle appearance (textures, colors) with dynamics (how things move). A model trained on driving will bias toward driving styles it saw, failing to transfer to new domains. This paper explicitly decouples them: learn appearance tokens (where do the pixels come from?) separately from action tokens (how do things move?), enabling cross-domain transfer without retraining.
VideoWorld 2.how:
The mechanism: Factorize the latent representation into appearance codes (VQ-encoded frames) and action tokens (discrete action embeddings). Train the diffusion model to predict: given appearance and action history, what's the next frame? The key: train on mixed domains (driving, robotics, animation) so the action space is unified. At test time, swap appearance tokens to change domain while keeping actions the same.

Why it works: Decoupling allows a single action semantics ("move forward", "turn left") to apply across embodiments and environments. Appearance transfer is straightforward (swap the visual texture). This eliminates the need for domain-specific world models, and one learned model can generate realistic consequences for the same action across driving, manipulation, and locomotion.

FlexTraj.narr: To steer a video diffusion model, you need to tell it where each object should go. But specifying dense keyframes is tedious. This paper lets users draw sparse or dense trajectories (point-and-click paths), and the model generates frames where the objects obey those paths—turning video diffusion into an interactive tool you can play like a game.
FlexTraj.how:
The mechanism: Encode trajectory information as a spatial guidance map (one channel per object, or a heatmap of the path). Condition the diffusion model on this guidance via cross-attention or concatenation. During generation, each denoising step respects the guidance: if the trajectory says the ball should be at (x, y) at frame t, the model learns to place it there.

Why it works: Trajectory conditioning is geometrically natural: humans reason in paths and positions, not pixel values. By embedding path constraints into the denoising loop, the model balances generation quality (photorealism) with control fidelity (object follows the path). The result is a simulator users can steer intuitively.

TGT: Text-Grounded Trajectories.narr: Natural language describes what things should do ("the car turns left, the pedestrian walks forward"), but images don't store language. This paper bridges them: text specifies per-object motions, which are compiled into spatial motion patterns that guide image-to-video generation, letting language directly control physical outcomes.
TGT: Text-Grounded Trajectories.how:
The mechanism: Parse language instructions into object-motion graphs (entity, verb, direction, duration). Render these into optical-flow-like fields or trajectory heatmaps. Condition the video diffusion model on these fields via cross-attention to text embeddings and guidance maps. During generation, the model learns to generate frames where objects follow the language-specified trajectories.

Why it works: Language is compositional—"A moves left, B moves right"—and spatiotemporal patterns (flow fields, trajectories) are the natural intermediate representation. By parsing language to geometry and then to pixels, the model respects both linguistic intent and visual plausibility. One text prompt steers multiple objects coherently.

LAMP.narr: Video diffusion is powerful but raw: it needs precise spatial coordinates or flow fields. Language models are powerful but abstract: they reason in tasks and goals. This paper stacks them: an LLM translates a user's request into a domain-specific language for camera and object motion, which is then fed to the video model, making it a programmable, deterministic simulator.
LAMP.how:
The mechanism: Define a DSL with primitives: camera(pan, zoom, position), object(trajectory, rotation, scale). Train an LLM on examples to map natural-language instructions to DSL programs. At generation time, parse the DSL into guidance signals (camera matrices, per-object paths, 3D transforms). Condition video diffusion on these structured signals.

Why it works: The DSL bridges semantic understanding (LLM's strength) and visual control (diffusion's strength). Determinism comes from precise DSL execution, not model sampling. Users get the fluidity of language input with the reproducibility of code, and the video model generates frames consistent with the structured plan.

Goal Force.narr: A video model can generate any visual future, but steering it to obey a particular goal (e.g., an object moving in a specific direction under a force) is hard. This paper teaches the model to interpret force overlays — visual arrows and vectors drawn on the input — as instructions for how the predicted scene should respond to physics.
Goal Force.how:
The mechanism: (1) During training, augment videos with rendered force overlays (arrows, colors at certain pixels indicating applied forces). (2) Train a diffusion model conditioned on both the context frames and those overlays. (3) At test time, draw force overlays on an image, and the model generates a future where objects respond to those forces. (4) The overlays are visual; the model learns their semantics.

Why it works: Force overlays are intuitive to draw and visually interpretable. By conditioning on them, the model learns an implicit physics model that respects the forces, turning video generation into a physics-aware simulator.

GaussianDWM.narr: A self-driving car needs to predict: "where will the other cars be? what space is free to drive?" and "what will that future look like?" Those are two separate problems—forecasting (geometry + motion) and rendering (appearance)—but most models conflate them. This paper explicitly decouples them using 3D Gaussians, and adds language conditioning for scenario description.
GaussianDWM.how:
The mechanism: Represent the scene as a set of 3D Gaussians (one per agent/object). Learn a dynamics model that predicts the Gaussians' positions and covariances at future timesteps. Separately, learn a rendering module that maps Gaussians to RGB. Condition both on language embeddings so the model can generate scenarios described in text. At inference, forecast Gaussians forward, render the predicted scene.

Why it works: Gaussians naturally represent 3D geometry (position, shape, covariance). By decoupling forecasting from rendering, the model stays accurate on geometry even if rendering is approximate. Language conditioning enables scenario grounding: users can describe "rain, heavy traffic, night" and the model adjusts both the motion predictions and the appearance. Forecasting is now interpretable (you can inspect the predicted positions) and composable.

GenieDrive.narr: Driving simulation requires precise control over what moves and where it's safe. This paper predicts 4D occupancy (space-time occupancy grid) first, then conditions video generation on it, ensuring that the generated video respects the predicted geometry: cars stay on roads, pedestrians don't teleport through walls.
GenieDrive.how:
The mechanism: Encode multi-camera input into a top-down occupancy grid (bird's-eye view, one channel per object class). Predict how this grid evolves under the ego's planned action. Feed the predicted occupancy sequence as guidance to a video diffusion model (via concatenation or cross-attention). During generation, the model learns to render frames consistent with the occupancy, ensuring plausible futures.

Why it works: Occupancy is a geometric bottleneck—if it's wrong, the video will be nonsensical (cars floating, collisions). By predicting occupancy first and conditioning video on it, the model is forced to respect geometry. Video generation becomes a rendering problem given fixed geometry, which is much easier to solve stably than end-to-end prediction. The ego's action directly changes occupancy, ensuring action-conditioned generation.

RenderWorld.narr: Self-driving needs to know both where things are (geometry) and where they're going (occupancy over time). This paper makes Gaussian splats self-supervise occupancy by rendering them into a top-down grid, then uses that grid to learn a world model that predicts future occupancy.
RenderWorld.how:
The mechanism: (1) Render a 3D Gaussian scene into a top-down 2D occupancy grid. (2) Train an autoregressive world model on those grids to predict the next timestep. (3) Use prediction errors from real observations to improve both the splats and the model.

Why it works: Gaussians naturally convert to occupancy through rendering, bridging the visual and predictive layers. The self-supervision loop keeps the geometry honest without needing explicit 3D annotations.

Let Occ Flow.narr: Self-supervised learning from unlabeled camera footage is the dream for autonomous vehicles—no manual labels needed. This paper predicts 3D occupancy and optical flow jointly and self-supervisedly: the model learns that consistent flow-based motion agrees with occupancy changes, and vice versa, grounding both to camera observations without labels.
Let Occ Flow.how:
The mechanism: Train an encoder-decoder on consecutive frames to predict 3D occupancy at t+1 and optical flow from t to t+1. Self-supervised losses: (1) warp occupancy by flow; compare to predicted next occupancy (consistency); (2) render flow as motion; compare warped frames (reprojection). No ground-truth occupancy or flow needed. Chain predictions forward for forecasting.

Why it works: Occupancy and flow are dual representations of motion. Occupancy says "cell (x,y,z) is occupied"; flow says "point moves by this vector." By enforcing consistency between them and checking against real observations, the model self-corrects. This breaks the dependency on expensive 3D labels, making it practical for in-the-wild driving data.

X-MOBILITY.narr: A robot navigating new buildings must adapt its predictions to new layouts. This paper learns a decoupled latent world model—the dynamics and the policy are separate modules—so the same dynamics model can serve different navigation policies, and a single learned model transfers zero-shot to new environments without retraining.
X-MOBILITY.how:
The mechanism: Learn an autoregressive latent dynamics model (given latent state and action, predict next state) from pretraining data (e.g., cross-embodiment video). Train a navigation policy separately. At test time on a new environment, collect a few rollouts (real interaction or in-sim exploration) to estimate latent state statistics. Use the pretrained dynamics for planning without updating it. If needed, adapt the policy but not the model.

Why it works: Decoupling means the model learns universal dynamics ("how does the world respond to actions?") while the policy learns task-specific ("how do I navigate to the goal?"). New environments have the same physics but different layouts, so the dynamics stay valid. Zero-shot transfer works because the latent space is geometry-agnostic: the model predicts motion consequences regardless of which building. Only the policy (if adapted) changes per environment.

RoboPack.narr: A robot packing a box must predict how soft objects deform under its gripper. Cloth and fabric don't follow rigid-body rules — they fold, bunch, and shift in ways hand-written physics can't capture. This paper learns that deformation from vision and touch, then uses model-predictive control to find the pack sequence that reaches the goal. The graph-based state (particles + edges) generalises across objects because it captures contact and topology directly.
RoboPack.how:
The state: represent cloth as a graph of particles connected by springs, read from RGB and tactile feedback.

  1. Forward pass: a recurrent graph neural network predicts the next particle positions given the current positions, action (gripper location/force), and edge topology.
  2. MPC loop: roll many candidate action sequences through the learned model, score each by distance to goal state, and execute the best first action.
  3. Online adaptation: observe the real outcome, compare to prediction, and quickly retrain the dynamics model if deformation differs — cloth is heterogeneous, so the model must adjust per object.

Graph structure lets the model transfer to new cloth sizes and configurations because the interaction rules (springs compress, collisions repel) are shared across all nodes, not locked to a specific shape.

High-Density Visual Particle Dynamics.narr: Bimanual manipulation moves hundreds of thousands of points at once — when both hands tug a rope or pull a bundle of cables, the scene is dense, tangled, and chaotic. Pixel-space prediction is intractable; a monolithic latent state blurs the contacts. This paper lifts the entire point cloud into a learned latent dynamics model, using transformers to predict how 100k+ particles move under dual-arm actions. The key insight: dense point geometry, not pixels, is the right substrate for deformable prediction.
High-Density Visual Particle Dynamics.how:
The state: point cloud (xyz coords + optionally features) of the deformable object.

  1. Encoding: a transformer encoder processes all 100k+ points, learning which ones interact (local attention) and predicting the next cloud conditioned on the dual-arm action.
  2. Prediction: output the new point positions directly. The transformer attends over the full cloud so it learns long-range tension (when you pull one end, the opposite end feels it).
  3. From state to control: use the predicted next state to score candidate trajectories; either pick the best sequence (planning) or use imagined rollouts as training data for a policy (learning in imagination).

Transformers on point clouds are permutation-invariant, so the model works on piles of different sizes and orientations without retraining. The dense representation forces the model to learn real contact mechanics instead of painting plausible pixels.

Dynamic 3D Gaussian Tracking for Neural.narr: Rope and cloth are continuous surfaces that twist, coil, and tangle under manipulation. A point cloud alone loses topology — are these points connected by thread, or free-floating? A 3D Gaussian splat, with its smooth coverage and geometric coherence, naturally captures that surface. This paper uses 3D Gaussians to represent the deformable object, couples them to a graph neural network for contact inference, and learns action-conditioned dynamics so a robot can predict and plan rope manipulation. The splat surface is both the rendered appearance and the physical state.
Dynamic 3D Gaussian Tracking for Neural.how:
The state: 3D Gaussian splat (position, covariance, spherical-harmonics color) anchoring physics particles underneath.

  1. Physics layer: a sparse graph of control points and edges (modeled as springs) lives in the same space as the splats, inferring cable and rope connectivity from the geometry.
  2. Prediction: the GNN predicts how those physics particles move under the action, then moves the Gaussians to match, ensuring the splat surface stays coherent and deformed correctly.
  3. Rendering check: render the predicted splat configuration and compare to observed images; rendering error helps calibrate the physics.
  4. Closed-loop planning: roll forward many action sequences, score by goal reach, and execute.

Splitting geometry (splats) from topology (GNN edges) means the model learns contact mechanics while staying synchronized to what the camera sees — a kind of differentiable physics inside appearance.

Cloth-Splatting.narr: Predicting cloth shape from images is hard because you need both geometry (3D folds) and appearance (texture, lighting). Classical approaches decouple them, losing the tight link between what the cloth looks like and where it actually is. This paper makes the cloth state itself directly optimisable from RGB by using differentiable Gaussian rendering. Given an RGB image and a candidate action, render the predicted cloth Gaussians and backprop the image-reconstruction error back to the state — no separate pose estimation needed. The differentiable renderer closes the loop between vision and geometry.
Cloth-Splatting.how:
The state: a set of 3D Gaussians (position, scale, rotation, appearance parameters) representing the cloth surface.

  1. Forward model: a learned dynamics head (MLP or attention) predicts the next Gaussian parameters (position and deformation) given current state and action.
  2. Rendering: using differentiable splatting (rasterize Gaussians to pixels with gradients), render the predicted state as an image.
  3. Optimization: compare rendered pixels to observed images; backpropagate pixel-reconstruction loss through the renderer and dynamics to refine both the state estimate and the action.
  4. Planning: sample action sequences, render each, score by goal-image match or visual metrics, execute the best first action.

Differentiable rendering means cloth state is defined by image-reconstruction, not a hand-engineered marker or pose. Contact and fold geometry fall out naturally because the renderer enforces geometric consistency with the camera.

Physically Embodied Gaussian Splatting.narr: A world model needs to predict both the look and the movement of a scene, but they can easily drift apart — the model predicts the geometry wrong and the rendering becomes inconsistent. This paper couples them by storing the scene as a pair: Gaussian splats for appearance and a shadow set of physics particles for motion.
Physically Embodied Gaussian Splatting.how:
The mechanism: At each step, the physics particles move according to the learned dynamics. The Gaussians are then repositioned to follow their particles. Finally, the splats are rendered and compared against the real camera image. The render-vs-observation error becomes a 'visual force' that nudges the particles back into agreement when they drift.

Why it works: By tying rendering to physics through this feedback loop, the state can predict the future and stay photorealistic simultaneously. The splats are not just pretty; they constrain the physics.

DGGT.narr: Autonomous driving sees a 4D world — objects moving in 3D space over time — but most reconstructions look at single frames or fail on dynamic scenes. This paper reconstructs the full 4D trajectory of a driving scene from unposed (unlabeled camera angles) images, giving a parametric 4D model that can be queried and rendered from any view.
DGGT.how:
The mechanism: (1) Take unposed multi-view images of a dynamic scene. (2) Learn a feed-forward network that directly predicts 4D Gaussians (position, appearance, deformation over time) that explain those images. (3) Render those 4D Gaussians from arbitrary viewpoints and times, comparing to the input images as supervision.

Why it works: Feed-forward prediction avoids the optimization bottleneck of per-scene fitting. By anchoring to image observations, the model learns both spatial and temporal consistency in one pass.

Differentiable Robot Rendering.narr: Training a policy from vision requires gradients from pixels all the way back to motor commands. But a physical robot's kinematics are discrete jumps — joint angles don't smoothly affect pixel changes. This paper renders the robot as Gaussians whose positions are differentiably tied to joint angles, letting gradient flow from images back to control.
Differentiable Robot Rendering.how:
The mechanism: (1) Represent the robot body as a set of 3D Gaussians, each anchored to a joint by forward kinematics. (2) When a joint angle changes, the Gaussians' positions update deterministically. (3) Render those Gaussians to compare against the camera. (4) Backprop the image error through rendering and kinematics to the joint commands.

Why it works: Differentiable kinematics + rendering create an end-to-end path from pixels to motor torques. The robot becomes part of the differentiable simulator.

Planning in 8 Tokens.narr: Predicting photoreal futures pixel-by-pixel is gorgeous but impossibly expensive—a world model would need thousands of forward passes to plan, making it useless for real-time control. This paper asks: do you actually need pixels to decide what to do? For control, the gist matters far more than the picture. The approach compresses the entire scene into eight discrete tokens—just enough semantic and spatial signal to predict and plan on, nothing more. Rolling these tokens forward is roughly 100× faster than rolling frames, because you never render.
Planning in 8 Tokens.how:
The problem: Video-diffusion world models are photoreal but run at ~1 Hz; planning needs 100+ rollouts per decision. Raw pixel prediction is a mismatch.

The mechanism: 1. Encode a video frame into a compact latent space. 2. Quantize the latent into a discrete codebook—8 tokens chosen from a learned vocabulary. 3. Train an autoregressive token-prediction model to forecast the next 8 tokens from current tokens + action. 4. Roll the tokens forward H steps; planning never touches the pixel decoder. 5. Decode back to pixels only if you need to visualize for a human.

Why it works: Tokens capture semantic and geometric essence without appearance. The prediction model is tiny and runs fast enough to evaluate thousands of hypothetical futures. The trade-off is intentional: loss of photorealism, gain of 100× speedup for planning and sim-to-real transfer.

TraceGen.narr: Most video world models are trained on visual data alone, but real robotics has both labeled robot demonstrations and vast unlabeled internet video. This paper bridges them by learning the world in a universal 3D trace space—trajectories and geometric primitives that appear in both robot and non-robot video. A single trace-space world model predicts how the 3D structure evolves, and rolls 50–600× faster than pixel models because tracing is sparse.
TraceGen.how:
The problem: Video diffusion works on internet data but requires millions of robot rollouts for sim-to-real. Pixel space is domain-specific; you can't draw on cross-embodiment video.

The mechanism: 1. Extract 3D traces from video: sparse point clouds, stick-figure poses, or optical-flow fields that capture motion geometry without appearance. 2. Train a transformer to predict the next trace sequence from current trace + action, cross-trained on both robot and internet video. 3. Because traces are sparse (10–100 tokens) instead of dense (thousands of pixels), one forward pass is 50–600× faster. 4. Decode trace back to pixels if rendering is needed.

Why it works: Traces are a common language across embodiments. A quadruped and a humanoid both have moving limbs; their traces look similar even if their pixels don't. This forces the model to learn structure, not surface, and enables zero-shot transfer to new bodies.

Motus.narr: Robot learning has abundant labeled trajectory data ("I pushed, the object moved"), but computer vision has vastly more unlabeled video ("Something happened"). This paper unifies them under one signal: optical flow—the visible motion field between frames. Flow is action-like (it responds to what the robot did) and agnostic to embodiment, so a single world model trained on flow can bridge robot and internet video, then predict the same flow field for planning.
Motus.how:
The problem: Labeled robot data is expensive; unlabeled video is abundant. But they live in different spaces—action-conditioned rollouts vs. static video—so you can't mix them.

The mechanism: 1. Compute optical flow between consecutive frames in any video, labeled or not. 2. Predict the next optical-flow field from current flow + action (or action-agnostic for unlabeled video by learning a flow-only model). 3. Train jointly on robot data (actions are labeled) and internet video (learn the action-irrelevant flow patterns). 4. At test time, predict flow conditioned on a proposed action; that flow tells you how the world responds.

Why it works: Flow is intermediate between pixels (too specific) and state (too abstract). It captures object motion, deformation, and occlusions without appearance, so it transfers across cameras, lighting, and embodiments. A single flow-prediction model serves both imitation (unlabeled video) and action-conditioned rollouts (labeled robot).

DreamSAC.narr: Neural networks are brilliant at fitting data but terrible at extrapolating far beyond it. A world model trained to predict 4 steps ahead might hallucinate physics-defying futures at step 10—objects speeding up, energy appearing from nowhere. This paper injects Hamiltonian structure into the learned dynamics, enforcing conservation of energy and momentum at the architecture level, so the model literally cannot dream up impossible physics even when rolling far into the future.
DreamSAC.how:
The problem: Learned dynamics models compound small errors over long rollouts; errors often violate physical laws (non-conservation, interpenetration). Past a certain horizon, predictions are fiction.

The mechanism: 1. Parameterize the world model as a Hamiltonian system: state is split into position and momentum, and dynamics are derived from a learned energy function H(q, p). 2. The learned H function must have certain symmetries (time-reversal invariance, translational invariance) baked in. 3. Predict the next state by numerically integrating the Hamiltonian equations; this automatically conserves total energy and respects symplectic structure. 4. Also enable symmetry exploration: if the system has rotational symmetry, the model can rotate the scene and recognize it as equivalent, aiding extrapolation.

Why it works: Hamiltonian dynamics guarantee energy conservation by construction, not by training signal. A model that conserves energy can drift in quantitative details but never in fundamental physics. This buys you longer, more trustworthy rollouts even far outside the training distribution.

NS-Diff.narr: Diffusion video models generate mesmerizing futures, but they can violate physical laws — fluids that gain energy, objects that overlap. This paper enforces Navier-Stokes (fluid dynamics) and jerk constraints directly in the diffusion's latent space via a learned reward that penalizes unphysical predictions.
NS-Diff.how:
The mechanism: (1) Train a video diffusion model as usual. (2) At inference, instead of pure denoising, add RL-style optimization: evaluate each denoising step against a physical-law penalty (divergence, energy conservation, jerk bounds). (3) Use gradients from that penalty to steer the denoising toward physically valid futures. (4) Result: a video that looks realistic and obeys physics.

Why it works: RL feedback during generation acts as a constraint. Physics penalties are differentiable, so the model learns to generate futures that satisfy them.

Physical Simulator In-the-Loop Video Gen.narr: Asking a learned model to predict future video while obeying physics is hard. This paper puts a real physics simulator inside the generation loop: as the diffusion denoises, it interleaves steps from a material-point-method simulator (for fluids and deformables), keeping predictions consistent with real dynamics.
Physical Simulator In-the-Loop Video Gen.how:
The mechanism: (1) Start from noise and partially denoise into a video frame. (2) Extract material state (particles, velocities) from that partial frame. (3) Run one or more simulator steps (MPM for granular/fluid dynamics). (4) Re-render the simulator state and use that as conditioning for the next denoise step. (5) Iterate: denoise, extract, simulate, re-render.

Why it works: The simulator guarantees correct physics for the materials it models. Interleaving it with learning lets the diffusion model handle appearance while the simulator handles dynamics.

LoL: Longer than Longer.narr: Generate video for 30 seconds, and transformers usually collapse: the room freezes in place, colors drift, or the same frame repeats. The problem is that attention at position 1000 can't efficiently "remember" what happened at position 1. This paper prevents collapse by introducing random jitter into the position encodings (RoPE), breaking the pathological frequencies that cause late-horizon forgetting. The result is 12-hour continuous video generation—longer than human attention—without the model losing track of the scene.
LoL: Longer than Longer.how:
The problem: Video diffusion transformers accumulate and forget over long sequences. Attention patterns become degenerate; the model stops tracking object identity and just paints plausible static images.

The mechanism: 1. Use rotary position embeddings (RoPE) to encode absolute position. 2. Add structured noise to the rotation angles—jitter sampled per head and per sequence, breaking synchronization across the attention pattern. 3. Train on very long sequences (~100k tokens, hours of video) so the model learns that position jitter is normal. 4. At generation, continue applying jitter; the model never gets locked into a pathological frequency that causes forgetting.

Why it works: The jitter desynchronizes the frequency harmonics that cause attention collapse. By preventing the model from settling into a fixed oscillation pattern, each frame stays anchored to the full history. The trade-off is that generated video drifts more slowly and subtly; the model sacrifices some coherence of fine details for the ability to run for hours without catastrophic forgetting.

TempoMaster.narr: Long video requires predicting thousands of frames, but modern video models predict one frame at a time, which scales poorly. This paper decouples the problem into coarse-to-fine generation: first predict the low-frame-rate keyframe skeleton (every 8th frame), then densify upward by predicting the intermediate frames. Predicting at keyframe rate is 8× fewer steps, so the whole rollout becomes tractable without collapsing.
TempoMaster.how:
The problem: Autoregressive frame prediction for hours means thousands of forward passes; error compounds and models forget.

The mechanism: 1. Partition the video into keyframes (every N frames) and intermediates. 2. Train a coarse model to predict keyframe-to-keyframe transitions. 3. For each keyframe pair, train a local densification model to fill in the intermediate frames, conditioned on the keyframes. 4. At generation, roll the coarse model forward (N× fewer steps), then densify each segment in parallel. 5. Because each segment is only N frames, the local model stays accurate and coherent.

Why it works: Keyframe prediction has lower information-theoretic cost (you only need to predict the big changes), so the model doesn't waste capacity on frame-to-frame flicker. Densification is a simpler, more local task. Together, they cut the number of autoregressive steps from H to H/N, which is the difference between feasible and infeasible for long video.

HoloCine.narr: Film editing teaches a lesson: a scene is not one long continuous take but a sequence of shots, each with its own angle and framing. This paper imports that structure into video generation: instead of one monolithic rollout, it generates a multi-shot narrative with per-shot control via windowed cross-attention. The model can then coordinate across shots—characters move consistently from shot A to shot B—while letting each shot be generated independently, cutting memory cost and enabling fine-grained directorial control.
HoloCine.how:
The problem: Long video models either collapse over hours or bloat in memory trying to attend the entire history.

The mechanism: 1. Divide the video into shots (scenes with consistent framing). 2. Use a shot-aware attention mechanism where each frame attends over a sliding window (the current shot) and a sparse set of keyframes from previous shots. 3. Train the model to generate coherent transitions: the model learns that when the camera cuts from shot A to B, objects should be where they would be if continuously present. 4. At generation time, generate shot 1 fully, then for shot 2 condition on the keyframes from shot 1, without attending the full shot-1 history.

Why it works: Windowing reduces attention complexity from O(H²) to O(W·H), where W is the window size. The model can attend long-range dependencies (character identity, plot continuity) sparsely, while attending local details (motion, lighting within a shot) densely. This mirrors how humans watch film—we track consistency across cuts without holding every frame in working memory.

Captain Safari.narr: Aggressive camera movement—panning, tilting, zooming—makes it hard for world models to stay coherent: the scene appears to deform or warp as the camera moves. This paper decouples motion from appearance by maintaining a pose-aligned 3D memory of the scene and rendering it from different camera poses on demand. The memory stays consistent as the camera moves, so the world doesn't distort, and you can shoot from any angle for hours without the model forgetting what the world looks like.
Captain Safari.how:
The problem: Video prediction in camera space is hard when the camera is moving; small errors compound and the scene appears to rubber-band.

The mechanism: 1. Maintain a 3D scene representation (voxel grid, Gaussian splats, or feature map) in world coordinates. 2. Track the camera pose (position, orientation) at each frame. 3. Render the scene from the current camera pose; compare to the real image and update the 3D memory where there's mismatch. 4. When predicting the next frame, first predict the next camera pose, then render the predicted 3D memory from that pose. 5. The 3D memory is updated conservatively (only where confident), so it stays stable.

Why it works: Separating the 3D world from the camera disentangles two independent variations (world state and viewing angle). The model predicts only the world, not the camera's view of it, which is much easier. Camera motion becomes a pose-tracking problem, not a content-generation problem. The 3D memory acts as a persistent anchor that the model can reference for hours without deformation.

Points2Plans.narr: To stack blocks or rearrange objects, a robot needs to predict how each object will move when it acts, not just the aggregate scene. But a flat latent state smears all objects together, so rearranging them confuses the model. This paper factors the world into composable relational dynamics—each object is a node, edges capture which objects interact, and a graph network predicts how each object responds. Rearrange the objects and the same interaction rules apply; the model generalizes to long-horizon multi-object tasks.
Points2Plans.how:
The problem: A monolithic latent world model can't generalize to new object arrangements; it memorized one spatial configuration, not the rules of interaction.

The mechanism: 1. Represent the scene as a point cloud (one 3D point per object) plus per-object properties (mass, color). 2. Build a graph: nodes are objects, edges connect nearby or potentially colliding objects. 3. Train a graph neural network to predict the next point cloud from the current points + action, passing messages along edges (each object updates based on its neighbors). 4. Because the interaction function is learned per-edge, it is agnostic to object count and spatial arrangement. 5. Chain predictions to plan a multi-object trajectory toward a goal.

Why it works: Shared interaction rules are the key to generalization. If the model learns "when two objects touch, they collide," that rule works whether there are 3 objects or 30, and whether they are in a line or a grid. A graph net factorizes the dynamics so the model learns reusable rules, not the memorized layout of one scene. This is what allows zero-shot transfer to new configurations and long-horizon planning.

Learning Differentiable Tensegrity Dynam.narr: A soft-rigid robot (cables, rods, springs) has structure that ordinary latent-state models completely miss. The cables are connected in specific ways, and when you pull one cable, only the connected part of the robot moves. This paper embeds the robot's structure into a graph neural network, so the model learns that pulling corner A affects only the nodes A is cabled to, not the whole robot. This makes predictions far more accurate and enables zero-shot transfer to different cable configurations.
Learning Differentiable Tensegrity Dynam.how:
The problem: Soft robots have rich structure (connectivity, constraints) that a generic dynamics model can't capture. Training requires thousands of rollouts.

The mechanism: 1. Define the robot as a graph: nodes are rigid segments or joints, edges are cables or springs with specific properties (stiffness, maximum length). 2. Embed this connectivity into a GNN: the message-passing rules respect the cable topology—a node only listens to its cabled neighbors. 3. At each step, predict node positions by passing messages along the graph (each cable transmits tension/compression to its endpoints). 4. Train on trajectories of one configuration; the learned edge functions are now reusable.

Why it works: The graph structure acts as a strong inductive bias. The model doesn't waste capacity on learning "what structure exists"; it already knows. So it learns faster from fewer data points, and the structure is baked in, making zero-shot transfer to different cable lengths or tensions possible. A purely latent model would need retraining.

NOD-TAMP.narr: Task-and-motion planning is hard because you need both a world model (what happens when I push?) and a task planner (what sequence of pushes gets me to the goal?). This paper unifies them using neural object descriptors—learned embeddings of object identity that stay consistent across viewpoints and time. A GNN-based world model operates on these descriptors, and a classical task planner reasons over them. Learn the descriptors from a few human demos, and the whole system generalizes to new scenes with new objects.
NOD-TAMP.how:
The problem: Task-and-motion planning usually requires hand-engineered object detectors and dynamics models. Real generalization needs learning, but learning from a few demos is hard.

The mechanism: 1. Learn a neural descriptor encoder from demos: objects are embedded into a dense vector space where similar objects are close. Descriptors are stable across camera angle and lighting. 2. Build a graph where nodes are object descriptors (e.g., [small, red, graspable]), edges are spatial relations. 3. Train a GNN to predict the next graph (how each object descriptor changes) when given an action. 4. Use a classical planner (e.g., PDDL) that reasons over this learned graph to find a sequence of actions that reaches the goal. 5. The planner's output trajectories are checked against the learned model; replanning occurs if the model predicts failure.

Why it works: Object descriptors abstract away appearance while preserving task-relevant semantics. A planner can reason over descriptors ("move small-red-object to zone-3") without seeing pixels, while the learned world model translates descriptor-level plans into pixel-level predictions. Few-shot learning of descriptors is easier than learning a full dynamics model, because you only need to capture object identity, not full physics.

MI-HGNN.narr: Predicting contact—when two objects touch—is critical for manipulation but hard to learn from pixels alone because contact is often hidden (fingers occlude the touch point). This paper embeds morphology (the robot's shape and structure) directly into the graph network, so the model has a geometric prior: "my gripper is 3 cm wide, so if I move it here, these two objects will collide." With this prior, contact perception improves dramatically using tiny parameter overhead.
MI-HGNN.how:
The problem: Learning contact from visual data is slow because contact is often occluded or happens at sub-pixel scale.

The mechanism: 1. Represent the robot morphology as a geometric graph: nodes are links or segments with known shapes (boxes, cylinders), edges are joints with known limits. 2. Build a scene graph combining the morphology graph and object point clouds. 3. Use a morphology-informed GNN where edge functions know the geometric constraints: if two nodes are connected by a rigid joint, they move together; if a link is a box, it has specific collision geometry. 4. When predicting the next state, the model uses this geometric prior to predict collisions before they appear in images. 5. Visual input corrects the prior, but the prior does most of the heavy lifting.

Why it works: Baking morphology into the graph is an inductive bias that dramatically reduces sample complexity. The model doesn't learn what the robot looks like from scratch; it already knows. So it can focus on learning object dynamics and contact, which is much faster and more accurate. The parameter cost is minimal because the morphology is fixed geometry, not learned.

RehearseVLA.narr: Vision-language-action policies are powerful ("pick up the red cube") but need hundreds of real-world demos to learn well. This paper short-circuits real data by using a geometry-aware world-model simulator to generate imagined rollouts and score whether they succeed. The policy trains on those imagined successes via offline RL, needing only 5 real demos to ground the simulator. Most of the learning happens in imagination, safe and fast.
RehearseVLA.how:
The problem: VLAs are data-hungry; real robot demos are expensive and slow to collect. How can you get the policy to practice without constant real interaction?

The mechanism: 1. Collect a small amount of real data (5 demos per task) and fit a geometry-aware world model to it: a model that predicts how objects move when the gripper acts, using 3D scene understanding. 2. For a language instruction (e.g., "stack the blue cube on the green cube"), run the VLA forward inside the simulator to generate imagined action sequences. 3. Roll each imagined sequence through the world model and check if the goal object ends up where the instruction asked. Successes are labeled with reward 1, failures with reward 0. 4. Train the VLA via offline RL (e.g., IQL or CQL) on the imagined rollouts and rewards, without touching the real robot. 5. Test on the real robot; the simulator's grounding on real data makes transfer efficient.

Why it works: A foundation VLA can already generate plausible action sequences; it just needs feedback on whether they succeed. The simulator provides that feedback, and because it is geometry-aware (not pixel-generative), it stays accurate over short horizons. Offline RL can refine the VLA's distribution over imagined successes without exploration noise. This trades visual diversity (simulator is limited) for sample efficiency (most learning is offline).

NIL: No-Data Imitation Learning.narr: Most imitation learning requires collecting human demonstrations, which is slow and expensive. This paper replaces human data with text-conditioned video diffusion—a generative model that takes a language instruction ("wipe the table") and generates a plausible video of a hand performing that task. The robot watches those imagined videos as demonstrations and learns to imitate them, without any collected human data. Remarkably, it works on real robots.
NIL: No-Data Imitation Learning.how:
The problem: Collecting 100+ robot demonstrations per skill is expensive. Can a general video model substitute?

The mechanism: 1. Use a pre-trained video diffusion model (trained on internet video of humans and robots) conditioned on language. 2. For a task (e.g., "pick up the cube"), prompt the diffusion model to generate 20 diverse videos of hands doing that task. 3. For each generated video, extract a sequence of frames showing the hand pose and object configuration over time. Treat this as a synthetic demonstration. 4. Use standard imitation learning (behavioral cloning or inverse models) to train a robot policy on these synthetic demonstrations. 5. Deploy on the real robot and fine-tune on a handful of real rollouts if needed.

Why it works: A video diffusion model, trained on billions of hours of internet video, has learned the space of plausible human and robot behaviors. When conditioned on language, it generates videos that are diverse, contextually appropriate, and often close to what a real robot needs to do. The robot policy learns from a distribution of plausible behaviors, which is more reliable than learning from a single human. The gap between internet video and robot embodiment is small enough that fine-tuning is minimal or unnecessary.

Dreamitate.narr: Instead of collecting human demonstrations, this paper fine-tunes a video-diffusion model on task videos (robot performing the skill) so it becomes a task-specific generator. Then the robot watches those generated videos and imitates them. The fine-tuned model encodes task knowledge—"here is what good wiping looks like"—in a compact generative model. The robot learns by watching its own model dream of success.
Dreamitate.how:
The problem: Imitation learning needs demonstrations, but collecting them at scale is expensive. Can you bootstrap a demonstration generator instead?

The mechanism: 1. Collect a few real task videos (robot successfully wiping, or stacking). 2. Fine-tune a pre-trained video diffusion model on these videos, conditioned on task embeddings or language. The model learns to generate task-specific futures. 3. At training time, prompt the fine-tuned model to generate a video of the task. Extract key waypoints (hand pose, object positions) from the generated video. 4. Train the robot policy via imitation to replicate those waypoints (behavioral cloning or inverse models). 5. The policy gets diverse, task-relevant demonstrations because the generative model interpolates between the few real videos and the broader distribution it learned from pre-training.

Why it works: Fine-tuning a video model is much cheaper than collecting 100+ demonstrations—you might use 10–20 real videos. The model learns a compressed representation of the task, and generates new variations on demand. Because the model is task-specific, its generations are more aligned to the robot than a generic internet-trained model. Imitation from a generative model also lets you implicitly teach uncertainty: the model's stochasticity means the policy sees different ways to accomplish the goal, leading to more reliable behavior.

SRPO.narr: Training a policy with a world model usually requires external reward functions, which are engineering-heavy and brittle. This paper learns rewards from the world model itself: represent the task goal as a latent embedding, roll imagined trajectories through the model, and score each trajectory by how close the imagined final state is to the goal embedding. The world model becomes both the simulator and the reward function. SRPO (state reward prediction via offline RL) optimizes the policy against these emergent rewards using only in-batch successes as signal.
SRPO.how:
The problem: Reward engineering is slow and error-prone. How do you define "success" without hand-writing a reward function?

The mechanism: 1. Train a world model (latent dynamics) to predict the next latent state from current state + action. 2. Learn a separate goal encoder that maps target images to goal embeddings in the same latent space. 3. For each batch of imagined rollouts, compute a trajectory score: the latent distance from the final predicted state to the goal embedding (small distance = high score). 4. Use an offline RL algorithm (e.g., CQL or IQL) to train the policy to maximize this latent-distance reward using only trajectories that achieved the goal as positive examples and failures as negative. 5. No external reward function; the world model and goal encoder define success implicitly.

Why it works: Latent-space distances are a natural similarity metric learned by the world model, so they align with task success. Because the reward is derived from the model's own representation space, it is consistent with what the model predicts. Using only in-batch successes as positive examples avoids reward hacking—the policy can only learn behaviors the model itself recognizes as valid. This eliminates reward engineering and transfers to new goals without retraining the core reward function.

Gameplay Filters.narr: Deploying a learned policy on a real robot is risky if the policy hasn't seen a dangerous situation before. This paper uses the world model to play out virtual adversaries in imagination: imagine a worst-case scenario, test whether the policy survives, and veto actions that lead to disaster.
Gameplay Filters.how:
The mechanism: (1) Before executing an action, imagine the next few steps. (2) In that imagined rollout, add virtual perturbations (adversarial forces, sensor noise, unexpected objects). (3) Evaluate whether the policy would still succeed or fail gracefully. (4) If the imagined worst case is too bad, veto the action and choose a safer alternative. (5) This filtering happens at inference time with no additional training.

Why it works: The world model lets you test actions against imaginary dangers. Adversarial rollouts stress-test the policy on scenarios too risky to try for real, providing a form of reliability without requiring labeled safety data.

World Models for Anomaly Detection in MB.narr: A learned world model expects the world to match its training distribution. On a real quadcopter, the moment a gust of wind or a mechanical fault happens, reality diverges from prediction. This paper uses that divergence as an anomaly signal: when prediction error exceeds a threshold, stop and switch to safe fallback.
World Models for Anomaly Detection in MB.how:
The mechanism: (1) Roll the learned model forward. (2) At each step, compare the predicted next state to what the sensors actually report. (3) Compute prediction error. (4) If error exceeds a learned threshold (tuned on held-out data), flag an anomaly. (5) When an anomaly is detected, stop the current policy and switch to a safe controller (hover, land, or return-to-home). (6) Optionally, log the anomaly and retrain the model.

Why it works: Prediction error is a sensitive indicator of distributional shift. By monitoring it, the model acts as a built-in safety filter without requiring explicit failure detection or hand-coded rules.

OCCUQ.narr: A 3D occupancy model predicts which voxels are filled or free, but it can be overconfident on unseen inputs. This paper estimates epistemic uncertainty in occupancy predictions efficiently, so planning knows which parts of the scene the model trusts and which need caution.
OCCUQ.how:
The mechanism: (1) Train an occupancy network with an ensemble or Bayesian head that outputs both a prediction and uncertainty. (2) Use an efficient approximation (e.g., Monte Carlo dropout or a learned uncertainty head) to avoid expensive ensemble inference. (3) Plan by preferring actions that keep the robot in high-confidence regions. (4) In low-confidence areas, use conservative collision buffers or request additional sensing.

Why it works: Epistemic uncertainty captures what the model doesn't know. By separating it from aleatoric noise, planning can be adaptive: confident in familiar areas, cautious in unseen ones.

UNREST.narr: Driving world models must handle stochastic actors (other vehicles with unpredictable intent) and sensor noise. This paper trains an uncertainty-aware decision transformer that predicts multiple plausible futures and chooses actions reliable to that uncertainty, rather than committing to a single best-case prediction.
UNREST.how:
The mechanism: (1) Train the world model to predict a distribution of futures, not a single deterministic trajectory. (2) Feed multiple rollouts (from that distribution) to the decision transformer along with their likelihoods. (3) The transformer learns to weight risky actions down and conservative actions up, based on scenario-conditional uncertainty. (4) Plan by selecting the action sequence that performs well across the distribution of plausible futures.

Why it works: By treating the future as uncertain and explicitly reasoning about multiple scenarios, the planner avoids optimizing for one lucky case and instead finds reliable, worst-case actions.

Learning to Walk from Three Minutes of R.narr: Sim-to-real transfer is hard because hand-built simulators miss the details that matter (foot compliance, friction variation, terrain deformation). This paper learns a residual dynamics model on just 3 minutes of real quadruped data: a physics engine predicts the bulk motion, and the learned residual corrects for what the physics engine misses.
Learning to Walk from Three Minutes of R.how:
The mechanism: (1) Record 3 minutes of real quadruped data (joint angles, IMU, terrain contact). (2) Compute what a standard physics simulator would predict for the same actions. (3) Fit a neural network to predict the residual: real_next_state - simulated_next_state. (4) Train a gait policy using the sum: simulator + learned residual. (5) Deploy on the real robot; the residual now accounts for unmodeled effects.

Why it works: Physics engines get the big picture right (gravity, inertia), so they need only a small correction. Learning just the residual from tiny amounts of real data is much easier than learning full dynamics. The simulator provides a strong prior.

Denoising World Model Learning.narr: Policies trained in a learned simulator often break on the real robot because the dream drifts from reality over long rollouts. This paper trains the policy in the simulator, then uses a denoising step to correct discrepancies: given a real observation, denoise it back to what the simulator 'would have seen', closing the sim-to-real gap from the policy's perspective.
Denoising World Model Learning.how:
The mechanism: (1) Learn a world model simulator from real data. (2) Train a policy in that simulator for as long as needed. (3) At deployment, when the policy acts on the real robot and observes a new state, run a denoising inverse model: map that real observation back to simulator-space. (4) Use the denoised (simulator-consistent) state for the next policy step. (5) This keeps the policy operating in familiar simulator space even though it's seeing real data.

Why it works: Denoising acts as a domain-adaptation layer. It doesn't change the policy; instead, it translates real observations into the simulator's language, so the policy can use its trained behavior without re-learning.

GRaD-Nav.narr: A drone needs to know whether it can fit through a gate before it flies at it, but computing that on the real robot is risky. This paper builds a differentiable 3D Gaussian splat simulator and trains a navigation policy inside it via differentiable rendering: gates are rendered, visibility is differentiable, and so gradients flow from gate-passing success back to control.
GRaD-Nav.how:
The mechanism: (1) Reconstruct the environment as 3D Gaussians (using structure-from-motion or NeRF). (2) Use a differentiable Gaussian renderer to project the scene into the drone's view. (3) Compute gate visibility and distance from the rendered image. (4) Train RL or MPC on a reward based on rendered gate proximity. (5) The differentiable renderer means gradients flow from goal (reach the gate) back to control (which direction to fly).

Why it works: Rendering is differentiable, so you can optimize control end-to-end from visual goals. The Gaussian scene is static but can be learned; the policy learns to navigate based on what the camera will see.

Beyond Simulation.narr: Most world models look great in videos but fail at the core task: predicting how the world responds to causal interventions. If you change the action, does the future meaningfully change, or does the model paint the same frames regardless? This paper builds metrics that catch models that look good but are actually just painting.
Beyond Simulation.how:
The mechanism: (1) Take a world model and a test scenario. (2) Feed it action A and record the predicted future. (3) Feed it a different action B and record that future. (4) Compute the difference: if the model is causal, A and B should produce significantly different futures. (5) If the futures are too similar, the model is not actually modeling causality, only painting frames. (6) Perturb the camera and check whether geometry is consistent across views. (7) Score across many perturbations to get a causality score.

Why it works: Causality is the core requirement for a world model (not just a video generator). Testing whether action changes lead to different futures reveals whether the model learned dynamics or just learned to paint plausible frames.

WorldLens.narr: Driving world models trade off between texture realism, geometric accuracy, and behavioral causality. A model might render pretty frames but place cars in the wrong lanes, or predict unrealistic motion. This paper builds a 12-metric suite that measures each of these independently, so you know exactly what each model trades off.
WorldLens.how:
The mechanism: (1) Collect ground-truth driving videos with annotations (lane positions, object trajectories, actions). (2) For each world model under test, generate future video. (3) Evaluate texture fidelity (LPIPS, FVD, etc.), geometry (object bounding box accuracy, camera consistency), and behavior (does the action cause the predicted changes?). (4) Report a score for each. (5) Visualize the trade-offs: a model might score high on texture but low on geometry.

Why it works: A single metric hides trade-offs. By evaluating texture, geometry, and behavior separately, you see exactly where each model strengths and weaknesses lie, guiding which to choose for which task.

Ref4D-VideoBench.narr: Video world models are proliferating, but there is no standard way to evaluate them. This paper proposes a 12-metric suite that tests semantics (do objects stay labeled correctly?), motion (is optical flow consistent?), temporal consistency (do changes persist?), and world knowledge (do physics and occlusions work?), grounding evaluation in what actually matters for planning and simulation.
Ref4D-VideoBench.how:
The mechanism: (1) Create or use existing video datasets with multi-level annotations (instance masks, optical flow, depth, action labels). (2) For each video model, generate a multi-frame prediction. (3) Compare semantics: do segmentation maps stay consistent? (4) Compare motion: does optical flow match? (5) Compare temporal consistency: do objects persist without popping? (6) Compare world knowledge: do physical constraints hold (occlusions, gravity)? (7) Report scores for all 12 metrics, so different models' strengths are visible.

Why it works: Benchmarking reveals what models actually do. Different tasks (planning, data augmentation, rendering) weight these metrics differently, so transparent evaluation guides model selection.

TiViBench.narr: Video world models need to support reasoning: a human watches a video and understands the structure of a plan, the geometry of a space, or the logic of a scenario. Can the model? This paper builds TiViBench to score how well video models support 'think-in-video' reasoning across structural, spatial, logical, and planning dimensions.
TiViBench.how:
The mechanism: (1) Collect diverse video reasoning tasks: compositional structure (does the model understand scenes are made of objects?), spatial reasoning (can it track occlusions and depth?), causal logic (do changes follow from actions?), and planning (can imagined futures support plan validity checks?). (2) For each task, generate a video prediction from the world model. (3) Run a reasoning test on it: can a classifier or a human judge whether the reasoning holds? (4) Report scores on each dimension. (5) This reveals whether the model predicts pixels that support reasoning, not just realistic-looking frames.

Why it works: Reasoning benchmarks measure utility, not just visual quality. A model might score high on FVD (realism) but low on spatial reasoning because it averages over object positions. TiViBench catches that disconnect.
